Need
nēd
n. & v. (want; necessity; to require; rendering Hebrew machcowr, Greek chreia)
From Saxon nead, necessity. Scripture treats need as the ordinary condition of the creature and the appointed occasion of supply, and it makes the confession of need the doorway to Christ's help.

Biblical Definition

Need is want that must be supplied from outside, and Scripture treats it as the creature's standing condition rather than an emergency. The Apostle answers it with a promise measured by God's riches instead of the need's size: “But my God shall supply all your need according to his riches in glory by Christ Jesus” (Philippians 4:19). The measure is the supply, not the shortfall. Our Lord forestalls anxious praying by locating the Father's knowledge before the request: “your Father knoweth what things ye have need of, before ye ask him” (Matthew 6:8), which does not abolish asking but changes its character from informing God to seeking Him. Need is also the appointed occasion for approaching the throne: “Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need” (Hebrews 4:16). Boldness and need go together, because the High Priest there is touched with the feeling of our infirmities. Most decisively, the confession of need is the condition of receiving Christ at all: “They that are whole have no need of the physician, but they that are sick: I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance” (Mark 2:17). Those who feel no need get no Physician.

Webster 1828 Definition

Want; occasion for something; necessity; a state requiring supply or relief. Scripture makes need the appointed occasion of grace, promises its full supply from God's riches, and makes the confession of need the condition of receiving the Physician.

expand to see more

NEED, n. [Sax. nead, necessity.] Want; occasion for something; necessity; a state that requires supply or relief.

2. Want of the means of subsistence; poverty; indigence; distress by poverty.

3. A time of distress; a difficulty; an exigency; as, a friend in need.

NEED, v.t. To want; to lack; to require, as supply or relief; as, we need food and raiment.

NEED, v.i. To be wanted; to be necessary; as, there needs no argument.

NEEDFUL, a. Necessary; requisite; needy; indigent. NEEDY, a. Distressed by want of the means of living.

Key Scripture

Philippians 4:19 — "But my God shall supply all your need according to his riches in glory by Christ Jesus."

Matthew 6:8 — "Be not ye therefore like unto them: for your Father knoweth what things ye have need of, before ye ask him."

Hebrews 4:16 — "Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need."

Mark 2:17 — "When Jesus heard it, he saith unto them, They that are whole have no need of the physician, but they that are sick: I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance."

Modern Corruption

Philippians 4:19 has been detached from its context of generosity and hardship and made a promise of prosperity, so that a verse about God supplying need is quoted to underwrite the pursuit of surplus.

expand to see more

Paul wrote Philippians 4:19 to a poor church that had just sent him money while he sat in prison, and immediately after saying he had learned to be content both to abound and to suffer need. The promise is that God will supply need, and the whole passage exists to define need against want and to detach contentment from circumstance. Prosperity preaching inverts every element of that setting: the promise is claimed by the comfortable rather than extended to the generous poor, need is quietly redefined as desire, and the contentment which is the chapter's explicit lesson is precisely what the doctrine makes impossible.

The opposite corruption is more respectable and equally damaging: a self-sufficiency that will not confess need at all. Mark 2:17 states the disqualification plainly — those who reckon themselves whole have no use for a physician, and Christ says He did not come to call them. That is not a description of some people who happen to be righteous; it is a description of people who think they are. Hebrews 4:16 shows the remedy in action, and the striking word in it is boldly. Need is not an embarrassment to be concealed before approaching God; it is the reason the throne is called a throne of grace.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew machcowr (want, need, poverty) governs the Proverbs' warnings; Greek chreia (need, necessity) is the New Testament noun of Philippians 4:19 and Hebrews 4:16.

expand to see more

Hebrew machcowr (H4270) — want, need, poverty; used of the need that comes upon the sluggard as an armed man.

Hebrew day (H1767) — enough, sufficiency; the measure God supplies to the poor brother in Deuteronomy.

Greek chreia (G5532) — need, necessity, want; the noun in “all your need” and “time of need”.

Greek hustereo (G5302) — to come short, to be in want; Paul's verb for suffering need in Philippians 4.

Greek autarkes (G842) — content, sufficient in oneself; the contentment Paul says he learned in every state.

Usage

"“My God shall supply all your need according to his riches” — the measure is the supply, not the shortfall."

"“Your Father knoweth what things ye have need of, before ye ask” — asking seeks God, it does not inform Him."

"“They that are whole have no need of the physician” — felt need is the condition of receiving Christ."
